go:422896.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 1

go:422894.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 3
go:422894.question:
Consider the following $\text{C}$ program. Assume parameters to a function are evaluated from right to left.

int h(int q) { printf("%d", q); return q; }

Choose the largest floating-point number among the following options.

B. $\begin{array}{|l|l|l|}\hline  \textbf{Sign} & \textbf{Exponent} & \textbf{Mantissa} \\\hline  \text{0} & \text{11111110} & \text{11111111111111111111111} \\\hline   \end{array}$

C. $\begin{array}{|l|l|l|}\hline  \textbf{Sign} & \textbf{Exponent} & \textbf{Mantissa} \\\hline  \text{0} & \text{11111111} & \text{11111111111111111111111} \\\hline   \end{array}$

D. $\begin{array}{|l|l|l|}\hline  \textbf{Sign} & \textbf{Exponent} & \textbf{Mantissa} \\\hline  \text{0} & \text{01111111} & \text{00000000000000000000000} \\\hline   \end{array}$

detailed_solution.markdown: By symmetry, 1 is before 2 in half of all permutations, so $P(X)=\frac12$; similarly $P(Y)=\frac12$. The relative order of {1,2} and the relative order of {3,4} involve different elements, and all 4 combinations (12/21 with 34/43) are equally likely, so $P(X\cap Y)=\frac14=P(X)P(Y)$ $\rightarrow$ independent. - Not mutually exclusive: 1 2 3 4 $\ldots$ satisfies both. - Neither must occur: 2 1 4 3 $\ldots$ satisfies none. - Equally likely, so X is not more likely than Y. Answer: X and Y are independent Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

go:422892.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 5
go:422892.question:
​​​​​Let $\text{T(n)}$ be the recurrence relation defined as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{l}
T(0)=1, \\
T(1)=2, \text { and } \\
T(n)=5 T(n-1)-6 T(n-2) \text { for } n \geq 2

\]

Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  3. $T(n)=\Theta\left(3^{n}\right)$
  4. $T(n)=\Theta\left(n 3^{n}\right)$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Cycle stealing: DMA takes one bus cycle and moves one word $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Burst mode keeps the bus for the whole block (no repeated bus requests), so it has higher throughput for bulk transfer $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt-driven I/O $\text{---}$ FALSE. In programmed I/O the CPU keeps polling the device status and wastes cycles; interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device interrupts. - Vectored interrupts give the ISR address directly (no polling to find the device), so ISR starts faster $\text{---}$ TRUE. Answer: Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt driven I/O (FALSE) Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

go:422885.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 12
go:422885.question:
​​​​Which one of the following regular expressions is equivalent to the language accepted by the $\text{DFA}$ given below?

  1. $0^{*} 1\left(0+10^{*} 1\right)^{*}$
  2. $0^{*}\left(10^{*} 11\right)^{*} 0^{*}$
  3. $0^{*} 1\left(010^{*} 1\right)^{*} 0^{*}$
  4. $0\left(1+0^{*} 10^{*} 1\right)^{*} 0^{*}$

detailed_solution.markdown: 1NF only requires every attribute value to be atomic (no multi-valued or composite attributes). - R can have a multi-attribute key $\text{---}$ TRUE (e.g. key (roll_no, course_id)). This is about keys, not about values. - R cannot have a foreign key $\text{---}$ FALSE, 1NF puts no restriction on foreign keys. - R cannot have a composite attribute $\text{---}$ TRUE, a composite attribute is non-atomic and must be split into simple attributes. - R cannot have more than one candidate key $\text{---}$ FALSE. Answer: R can have a multi-attribute key; R cannot have a composite attribute Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

go:422884.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 13
go:422884.question:
​Node $\text{X}$ has a $\text{TCP}$ connection open to node $\text{Y}$. The packets from $\text{X}$ to $\text{Y}$ go through an intermediate $\text{IP}$ router $\mathrm{R}$. Ethernet switch $\mathrm{S}$ is the first switch on the network path between $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{R}$. Consider a packet sent from $\mathrm{X}$ to $\mathrm{Y}$ over this connection.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the destination $\text{IP}$ and $\text{MAC}$ addresses on this packet at the time it leaves $\mathrm{X}$?

  1. The destination $\text{IP}$ address is the $\text{IP}$ address of $\text{R}$
  2. The destination $\text{IP}$ address is the $\text{IP}$ address of $\text{Y}$
  3. The destination $\text{MAC}$ address is the $\text{MAC}$ address of $\mathrm{S}$
  4. The destination $\text{MAC}$ address is the $\text{MAC}$ address of $\mathrm{Y}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - $L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\phi$ only means $L_1\subseteq L_2$. Equality also needs $L_2\subseteq L_1$ $\text{---}$ FALSE. - $L_1\cup L_3$ can be regular: take $L_1=\Sigma^*$, then $L_1\cup L_3=\Sigma^*$ $\text{---}$ FALSE (not always). - If $\overline{L_3}$ were regular, then its complement $L_3$ would be regular (closure under complement). So $\overline{L_3}$ is not regular $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so $\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}$ is regular $\text{---}$ TRUE. Answer: $\overline{L_3}$ is not regular; $\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}$ is regular Therefore, the correct option(s) are **B**.

go:422883.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 14

  2. Translate a virtual address to a physical address using the page table

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Threads can also be implemented in user space (user-level threads) $\text{---}$ FALSE. - The file descriptor table belongs to the process and is shared by all its threads $\text{---}$ FALSE. - Every thread has its own stack (and registers, PC) $\text{---}$ FALSE. - Threads share the same address space, so one thread can read/overwrite another thread's data; there is no protection between them $\text{---}$ TRUE. go:422882.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 15
go:422882.question:
​​​​Consider a process $\text{P}$ running on a $\text{CPU}$. Which one or more of the following events will always trigger a context switch by the $\text{OS}$ that results in process $\mathrm{P}$ moving to a non-running state (e.g., ready, blocked)?

  1. $\text{P}$ makes a blocking system call to read a block of data from the disk
  2. $\text{P}$ tries to access a page that is in the swap space, triggering a page fault
  3. An interrupt is raised by the disk to deliver data requested by some other process
  4. A timer interrupt is raised by the hardware

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Running $\rightarrow$ Ready: possible (preemption / time slice over). - Waiting $\rightarrow$ Running: NOT possible. When the I/O finishes, the process goes to Ready; only the scheduler can move it to Running. - Ready $\rightarrow$ Waiting: NOT possible. A process can block (request I/O) only while it is running. - Running $\rightarrow$ Terminated: possible (exit). Answer: Waiting to Running, Ready to Waiting Therefore, the correct option(s) are **A,B**.

go:422874.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 23

​​​Consider the following $\mathrm{C}$ function definition.

char *b =  a;

while (*b)

b++;

return b - a; }

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  2. Assuming a character array $c$ is declared as char $c[ ]=$ "abcd" in main ( ), the function call $fX$ (c) will always return a value
  3. The code of the function will not compile

detailed_solution.markdown: Precedence: + (highest) $\gt$ $-$ $\gt$ * $\gt$ / (lowest). Then $-$ is right associative: $9-(4-(7-6))=9-(4-1)=6$. / is right associative: $18/(6/2)=18/3=6$. Answer: 6 Therefore, the correct option(s) are **A,B,D**.

go:422871.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 26

​​​​​What is the output of the following $\text{C}$ program?

go:422867.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 30
go:422867.question:
Consider the following context-free grammar where the start symbol is $\text{S}$ and the set of terminals is $\{a, b, c, d\}$.
$$
\begin{array}{l}
S \rightarrow A a A b \mid B b B a \\
A \rightarrow c S \mid \epsilon \\
B \rightarrow d S \mid \epsilon
\end{array}
$$
The following is a partially-filled $\text{LL}(1)$ parsing table.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline
&a&b&c&d&\$ \\ \hline
S &S\rightarrow AaAb &S\rightarrow BbBa &\text{(1)} & \text{(2)} & \\ \hline
A & A \rightarrow \varepsilon &\text{(3)} & A\rightarrow cS& &  \\ \hline
B & \text{(4)} &{B \rightarrow  \varepsilon} & &B\rightarrow dS& \\ \hline
\end{array}$

Which one of the following options represents the CORRECT combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table?

Note: In the options, "blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty.

  1. $(1)$ $S \rightarrow A a A b$ $(2)$ $S \rightarrow B b B a$ $(3)$ $A \rightarrow \epsilon$ $(4)$ $B \rightarrow \epsilon$
  2. $(1)$ $S \rightarrow B b B a$ $(2)$ $S \rightarrow A a A b$ $(3)$ $A \rightarrow \epsilon$ $(4)$ $B \rightarrow \epsilon$
  3. $(1)$ $S \rightarrow A a A b$ $(2)$ $S \rightarrow B b B a$ $(3)$ blank $(4)$ blank
  4. $(1)$ $S \rightarrow B b B a$ $(2)$ $S \rightarrow A a A b$ $(3)$ blank $(4)$ blank

detailed_solution.markdown: Final a depends only on which a-update runs first; final b only on which b-update runs first. - a: $(1+1)\times2=4$ if T1's update is first, $2\times1+1=3$ otherwise. - b: $(1+1)\times2=4$ if T1's update is first, $3$ otherwise. - T1 then T2: (4, 4). T2 then T1: (3, 3). - T1: a=a+1, T2: b=2b, T2: a=2a, T1: b=b+1 $\rightarrow$ (4, 3). - (3, 4) is impossible: it needs T2's a-update before T1's a-update and T1's b-update before T2's b-update. But in program order T1 does a before b and T2 does b before a, so this creates a cycle. Answer: (a=4, b=4); (a=3, b=3); (a=4, b=3) Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

Heap: [131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82] Answer: 131, 111, 90 Therefore, the correct answer is **Option B**.

go:422865.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 32
go:422865.question:
​​​​Consider an array $\mathrm{X}$ that contains $\mathrm{n}$ positive integers. A subarray of $\mathrm{X}$ is defined to be a sequence of array locations with consecutive indices.

The $\mathrm{C}$ code snippet given below has been written to compute the length of the longest subarray of $\mathrm{X}$ that contains at most two distinct integers. The code has two missing expressions labelled $\text{(P)}$ and $\text{(Q)}$.

int first=0, second=0, len1=0, len2=0, maxlen=0;
for (int i=0; i < n; i++) {
    if (X[i] == first) {
        len2++; len1++;
    } else if (X[i] == second) {
        len2++;
        len1 = (P); 

        second = first;
    } else {
        len2 = (Q);
        
        len1 = 1; second = first;
    }
    if (len2 > maxlen) {
        maxlen = len2;
    }
    first = X[i];
}

Which one of the following options gives the CORRECT missing expressions?

(Hint: At the end of the $i$-th iteration, the value of $len 1$ is the length of the longest subarray ending with $\mathrm{X}[i]$ that contains all equal values, and $len 2$ is the length of the longest subarray ending with $\mathrm{X}[i]$ that contains at most two distinct values.)

  1. $\text{(P) }  \text{len} 1+1$       $\text{(Q) } \text{len} 2+1$
  2. $\text {(P) } 1$                    $\text{(Q) } \text{len} 1+1$
  3. $\text{(P) } 1$                    $\text{(Q) }  \text{len} 2+1$
  4. $\text{(P) } \text{len} 2+1$       $\text{(Q) } \text{len} 1+1$

detailed_solution.markdown: Divide both sides by $n$: $\frac{T(n)}{n}=\frac{T(\sqrt n)}{\sqrt n}+1$. Let $S(n)=\frac{T(n)}{n}$. Then $S(n)=S(\sqrt n)+1$. Taking square roots repeatedly, $n\to n^{1/2}\to n^{1/4}\to\cdots$ reaches a constant after $\log\log n$ steps, adding 1 each step. So $S(n)=\Theta(\log\log n)$. $T(n)=n\,S(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)$ Answer: $T(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)$ Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

go:422863.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 34
go:422863.question:
Let $x$ and $y$ be random variables, not necessarily independent, that take real values in the interval $[0,1]$. Let $z=x y$ and let the mean values of $x, y, z$ be $\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z}$, respectively. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. $\bar{z}=\bar{x} \bar{y}$
  2. $\bar{z} \leq \bar{x} \bar{y}$
  3. $\bar{z} \geq \bar{x} \bar{y}$
  4. $\bar{z} \leq \bar{x}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - $(X,Y)\rightarrow(Z,W)$ does not give $X\rightarrow(Z,W)$; Y may be required $\text{---}$ FALSE. - Decomposition rule: $XY\rightarrow ZW$ $\Rightarrow$ $XY\rightarrow Z$ $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Pseudo-transitivity: $W\rightarrow Y$ $\Rightarrow$ $XW\rightarrow XY$ (augment by X), and $XY\rightarrow Z$, so $XW\rightarrow Z$ $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Transitivity: $X\rightarrow Y,\;Y\rightarrow Z$ $\Rightarrow$ $X\rightarrow Z$ $\text{---}$ TRUE. Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4 Therefore, the correct answer is **Option D**.

go:422862.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 35
go:422862.question:
​​​​​The relation schema, Person (pid, city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

To find the list of cities where at least $3$ persons reside, using the above operators, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is

  1. $1$
  2. $2$
  3. $3$
  4. $4$

detailed_solution.markdown: In a BFS tree, every edge $u\rightarrow w$ of G satisfies $level(w)\le level(u)+1$. A forward edge goes from $u$ to a non-child descendant $w$, so $level(w)\ge level(u)+2$ $\text{---}$ this contradicts BFS. Hence there are no forward edges $\text{---}$ TRUE. The others can fail: - Back edge: G = {v$\rightarrow$a, a$\rightarrow$v}. Tree {v$\rightarrow$a} is both DFS and BFS tree; a$\rightarrow$v is a back edge. - Cross edge: G = {v$\rightarrow$a, v$\rightarrow$b, b$\rightarrow$a}. DFS visits a then b; b$\rightarrow$a is a cross edge, and the tree is also the BFS tree. - So G can also have edges outside T. Answer: There are no forward-edges in G with respect to T Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

go:422861.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 36
go:422861.question:
​​​​​Consider a multi-threaded program with two threads $\mathrm{T} 1$ and $\mathrm{T} 2$. The threads share two semaphores: $s1$ (initialized to $1$) and $s2$ (initialized to $0$). The threads also share a global variable $\mathrm{x}$ (initialized to $0$). The threads execute the code shown below.

//code of T 1
wait (s1);
x = x+1;
print (x);
wait (s2);
signal(s1);
// code of T2
wait (s1);
x= x+1;
print (x) ;
signal (s2);
signal (s1);


Which of the following outcomes is/are possible when threads $\mathrm{T} 1$ and $\mathrm{T} 2$ execute concurrently?

  2. $\mathrm{T} 2$ runs first and prints $1, \mathrm{~T} 1$ runs next and prints $2$
  3. $\text{T1}$ runs first and prints $1, \text{T 2}$ does not print anything (deadlock)
  4. $\mathrm{T} 2$ runs first and prints $1, \mathrm{~T} 1$ does not print anything (deadlock)

detailed_solution.markdown: Conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write): - z: only T1 uses it $\rightarrow$ T1 has no conflict with anyone. - x: only T2 uses it. - y: $r_3(y),w_3(y)$ come before $r_2(y),w_2(y)$ $\rightarrow$ T3 must come before T2. So any serial order with T3 before T2 is conflict equivalent, and T1 can be anywhere: $T_1T_3T_2,\;T_3T_2T_1,\;T_3T_1T_2$. $T_1T_2T_3$ puts T2 before T3 $\rightarrow$ not equivalent. Answer: $T_1T_3T_2$, $T_3T_2T_1$, $T_3T_1T_2$ Therefore, the correct option(s) are **B,C**.

go:422860.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 2 | Question: 37

detailed_solution.markdown: Minterms 3, 5, 6, 7 = 011, 101, 110, 111 $\rightarrow$ F = 1 when at least two inputs are 1 (majority function). - Maxterms are the remaining combinations: $\Pi(0,1,2,4)$ $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Majority function $=XY+YZ+XZ$ $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Depends on Y: $F(1,0,0)=0$ but $F(1,1,0)=1$ $\text{---}$ so not independent of Y. - Depends on X: $F(0,1,0)=0$ but $F(1,1,0)=1$ $\text{---}$ so not independent of X. detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Complete subgraph of size k: FALSE. The 5-cycle $C_5$ has $\chi=3$ but no triangle. - Independent set of size $\ge n/k$: TRUE.
